extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and Office personnel (and patent prosecutors/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and documenting obviousness rejections under §103, including required factual findings and situational rationales (use of known techniques, predictable results, and 'obvious to try'). Directed at examiners evaluating claims in light of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on a stated rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a precondition repeatedly stated for each rationale; whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, must be articulated to explain a conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (Methods, or Products) — Required Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a “base” device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an “improvement;” (2) a finding that the prior art contained a “comparable” device (method, or product that is not the same as the base device) that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have applied the known “improvement” technique in the same way to the “base” device (method, or product) and the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a particular class of devices has become part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art based on teaching of such improvement in other situations. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used to support obviousness. The Supreme Court in KSR noted that if the actual application would have been beyond the skill of one of ordinary skill, then using the technique would not have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement — Required Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a “base” device (method, or product) upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an “improvement;” (2) a finding that the prior art contained a known technique that is applicable to the base device (method, or product); (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and resulted in an improved system; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: when a particular known technique is part of the ordinary capabilities of the skilled artisan and the base device was ready for improvement, applying the technique producing predictable results can support obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Obvious to Try” — Required Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) a finding that at the time of the invention, there had been a recognized problem or need in the art, which may include a design need or market pressure to solve a problem; (2) a finding that there had been a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the recognized need or problem; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale supports obviousness where a person of ordinary skill would pursue known, finite, predictable options with a reasonable expectation of success (KSR). If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used. The test emphasizes predictability and reasonable expectation of success; mere existence of many options is not dispositive if prior art narrows them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and predictability factors for applying “obvious to try” (case-law constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must consider the characteristics of the science/technology, its state of advance, the nature of the known choices, the specificity/generality of the prior art, and the predictability of results in the area of interest (Abbott Labs v. Sandoz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law cautions: (a) 'finite' means a small or easily traversed number of options in the context of the art (Takeda, Rolls‑Royce); (b) obvious-to-try is improper when it would require trying numerous parameter variations with no indication which are critical, or when it would be exploring a new technology with only general guidance (Kubin citing O'Farrell); (c) unpredictability in the art (e.g., therapeutic/isomer outcomes) can defeat an obvious-to-try argument (Sanofi, Bayer, Ortho‑McNeil examples). Examiners should place the inquiry in the context of the specific subject matter and decide on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound selection — flexible lead compound test
rubrics_metrics.description: A restrictive view requiring the prior art to point to only a single lead compound is improper; the lead compound test should be flexible and preliminary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit rejected a rigid lead-compound requirement (analogous to TSM) in favor of a flexible approach: evidence that a prior-art set of compounds included more potent candidates, that the examiner considered the compounds relevant, or expert testimony that one of ordinary skill would select certain compounds can support a conclusion that a skilled artisan would have used such compounds as a starting point. Findings that a compound was a natural choice for development support obviousness; however, absence of reason to select a particular lead compound may negate an obviousness rejection (Takeda, Ortho‑McNeil).
